Probably not. An S&P 500 fund is diversified across companies, but it's a single asset class: all U.S. large-cap stocks, with the top handful of tech names a large share of the index. It has fallen about 50% twice since 2000 (2000-02 and 2008-09), and 2000-2009 returned roughly nothing in total. At 56, with retirement perhaps 10 years away, a drop like that late in your accumulation phase, or early in withdrawals, can permanently shrink your retirement income (sequence-of-returns risk), because you may have no time to recover and may have to sell at lows.

The strongest case for it is that stocks have beaten bonds over nearly every long holding period, and a retirement lasting 30+ years still needs growth. That argues for keeping substantial equity exposure, not 100%. A common range at your age is roughly 50-70% stocks, with the rest in bonds or cash-like assets, and some international stocks within the equity portion.

What would flip my view: a pension or Social Security that covers essential expenses, a large cushion beyond what you need, flexibility to work longer or cut spending in a crash, and a history of actually holding through a 40-50% decline without selling. If all of those apply, a high equity share is defensible.

If this involves selling holdings in a taxable account, taxes on gains are a separate cost to check. Inside an IRA or 401(k) there are none. A fee-only fiduciary advisor can test the allocation against your actual income needs and timeline.
